These questions are useful because audiences rarely need every row of data. They need a smaller, meaningful summary.

7.2 Counts
A count is the number of observations that meet a condition.
Counts are the foundation of many summaries.
Examples:

How many students are in the file?

How many tutoring appointments were completed?

How many missing grades appear?

The key question is:

What exactly is being counted?

Counting rows may or may not answer the question.
If one row is one student, row count may count students. If one row is one tutoring appointment, row count counts appointments, not students.

A percentage describes a part as a share of a whole.
The basic idea is:
\[

7.4 Denominators
The denominator is the whole group used to calculate a percentage, rate, or average.
In the formula below, the denominator is the bottom number:

\]
Different denominators create different meanings.

title: 7  Descriptive Summaries
text:
7.9 Writing Interpretations
A table does not speak for itself.
After a summary table, write a short interpretation.
A useful interpretation usually includes:

the source or cleaned dataset;
the main comparison or pattern;
the denominator or group size;
the unit;
a caveat when needed.

Example:

In the cleaned Spring 2027 tutoring file, 48 of the 51 students with at least one completed tutoring visit had a recorded final grade. Their average recorded final grade was 84.6 points, compared with 78.4 points among the 76 students with recorded grades and no recorded tutoring visits. This comparison is descriptive and does not show whether tutoring caused the grade difference.

This paragraph is longer than “tutoring worked,” but it is much more responsible.






TipA useful sentence frame



In [source/time frame], [group or denominator] had [summary value], compared with [comparison value]. This means [careful interpretation], but [caveat].

7.10 Descriptive Summaries in Quarto
Students can include descriptive summaries in Quarto as typed markdown tables, code output, or a combination of both.
For a hand-built table:
| Tutoring Use Group | Students in Group | Average Recorded Final Grade |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| No recorded tutoring visit | 82 | 78.4 points |
| At least one completed tutoring visit | 51 | 84.6 points |
For an R workflow, a grouped summary might look like this:
summary_table <- tutoring_clean |>
  dplyr::group_by(visited_tutoring) |>
  dplyr::summarize(
    students = dplyr::n_distinct(student_key),
    students_with_grade = sum(!is.na(final_grade)),
    average_grade = mean(final_grade, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
The code creates a table. The communication work is deciding whether the table has the right rows, columns, labels, denominators, and caveat.

7.11 Checking a Summary
Before using a summary in a memo, check it.
Ask:

What is the unit of observation?
What is being counted?
What is the denominator?
Are missing values included, excluded, or described?
Are group labels audience-readable?
Does the table show counts as well as percentages when needed?
Does the interpretation stay descriptive?
Does the caveat match the cleaning log and data dictionary?

One helpful habit is to compare a summary table to the cleaning log.







Cleaning Log Issue
Summary Check




999 recoded as missing
Does the summary exclude those values from averages?


Appointment labels cleaned
Do table rows use the cleaned labels?


Missing grades documented
Does the table show how many grades were available?


Visit count recoded to yes/no
Does interpretation avoid pretending frequency was preserved?



The summary should not hide important cleaning decisions.

title: 7  Descriptive Summaries
text:
7.13 Common Problems to Watch For
Descriptive summaries often go wrong in predictable ways.







Problem
Why It Matters




Count rows when the claim is about people
The same person may appear more than once.


Report a percentage without a denominator
The audience cannot tell what group is being described.


Compare counts across groups of different sizes
Larger groups may have larger counts even if the rate is lower.


Hide missing values
The summary may describe only records with available data.


Use raw codes in a table
The audience may not understand the categories.


Average identifiers
Software can calculate meaningless results.


Use too many decimal places
The number may look more precise than the data support.


Use descriptive evidence for a causal claim
The claim is stronger than the summary supports.



Most of these problems can be fixed by returning to the data dictionary, cleaning log, and audience question.

title: 7  Descriptive Summaries
text:
7.14 Practical Workflow
Use this workflow when creating a descriptive summary:

Name the audience question.
Identify the unit of observation.
Choose the variables needed for the summary.
Check the data dictionary.
Check the cleaning log.
Decide whether you need a count, percentage, rate, average, or grouped summary.
Identify the numerator and denominator.
Build the summary table.
Check missing values and group sizes.
Write a short descriptive interpretation.
Add a caveat when the summary could be overstated.
Document any AI help and verification.

The workflow keeps the summary connected to meaning instead of letting the table become detached from the data.

Descriptions:

TipSolutions






A descriptive summary is a count, percentage, rate, average, table, or comparison that describes what is in the data.
Counting rows depends on the unit of observation. If one person can appear in multiple rows, row counts may count events, visits, transactions, or records rather than unique people.
A denominator is the whole group used to calculate a percentage, rate, or average.
The denominator tells the audience what group is being described. Without it, a percentage can be unclear or misleading.
A rate can be more useful when groups have different sizes. For example, visits per 100 students may be more useful than total visits when comparing campuses with different enrollments.
The mean is the arithmetic average. The median is the middle value after sorting. They can differ when a variable has very large or very small values.
Group sizes help the audience interpret the comparison. They also make missing data and small groups easier to notice.
One careful interpretation is: In the cleaned Spring 2027 tutoring file, students with at least one completed tutoring visit had an average recorded final grade of 84.6 points, compared with 78.4 points for students with no recorded tutoring visit. This comparison is descriptive and does not show whether tutoring caused the difference.
Useful AI tasks include drafting code from verified variable definitions, checking whether denominators are named, or revising an interpretation for clarity. Risky AI tasks include inventing numbers, guessing denominators, or turning a descriptive comparison into a causal claim.
